Load this before you write or change a `.tf` or `*.turf.hcl` file: a configuration from a request in plain language ("create an S3 bucket", "use the Azure AVM disk module"), an edit the user asked for, or an overlay that adds an interaction point. [`skill_deployment`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/) comes first in any session: it runs what you write — the convergence, approval, turf actions, recovery. Setting variable values (`var`, `var_file`, a `.tfvars` line) is deployment, not authoring.

Turf has no authoring tools. The configuration directory is the desired state, and every plan is a projection of whatever its files say, so the files you write *are* the declaration: the user can read them, check them into git, run them anywhere Terraform runs, and reopen them next session. You already know HCL; this skill covers the loop around it and where Turf differs.

**No file tool?** Say so plainly: Turf can still run an existing configuration — plan, apply, destroy, import, refresh, run actions — but writing one needs a file tool.

## The loop

```
init({ path: "/path/to/app" })   # register the directory; an absent one is created (with a .gitignore)
  …write versions.tf, main.tf…   # your file tools
init({ path: "/path/to/app" })   # again once providers and modules are written: installs them
open({})                         # the backend comes from the files
up({ var: { … } })               # the plan of the whole directory, paused at its approval point
  …edit → up again               # each up supersedes the paused convergence
apply({ convergence_id: "…", plan_digest: "…" })   # after review and approval, as skill_deployment says
```

- **Every plan is the whole directory.** To change a plan, edit the files and `up` again. There is no per-resource planning call.
- **Never edit between `up` and `apply`.** The engine checks the files again before applying; a plan whose files changed is never applied (it ends `stale`). Edit, `up`, then approve the new plan.
- **Re-run `init` after adding a `module` block or a provider** (one an overlay's action needs included): it installs them and updates the lock file.
- **Errors name a file and line.** Fix the file and `up` again; read each round's `diagnostics` too.
- **Don't rewrite the configuration to force convergence.** A deferral resolves by applying and planning the next round, which `apply` does by itself — not by hard-coding a value or splitting the work.

## Before writing: discover

- **`provider_search`** to find a provider; **`provider_describe`** for the exact schema of a `resource_type`, `datasource_type` or `action_type` — required arguments, nested blocks, which attributes are `write_only`, and the `identity_schema` an import can use — or of one provider-defined `function`, called as `provider::<local name>::<function>(…)` from a module whose `required_providers` declares the provider (each module declares its own; the built-in one as `terraform = { source = "terraform.io/builtin/terraform" }`, whose `encode_tfvars`, `decode_tfvars` and `encode_expr` are in the Terraform documentation, not `provider_describe`). Write from the schema, not from memory: provider schemas drift between versions. Pin the version in `versions.tf` and run `init` first, then describe the version `init` resolved (`providers[]`), so the schema is the one that will run.
- **A module's interface is in its files.** Write the `module` block with just `source` (and `version` for a registry source), run `init`, and read the installed module: `modules/modules.json` under the `data_dir` `init` reports (`.terraform`, unless `TF_DATA_DIR` moves it) maps each call to its directory (a local source is read in place). Its `variable` blocks are the inputs (no `default` = required), its `output` blocks what it exposes, its `required_providers` what it needs — `configuration_aliases` there means the call passes those slots in `providers = { … }`.
- **To look something up**, declare a `data` block and read the value from the plan document ([`references/data-sources.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/data-sources/)).

## Writing the files

A conventional layout, which Turf does not require but users expect:

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `versions.tf` | `terraform { required_providers { … }  backend "…" { … } }` — pin each provider (`~> MAJOR.MINOR`) |
| `providers.tf` | `provider {}` blocks — one per aliased instance |
| `variables.tf` | `variable {}` blocks |
| `main.tf` (or one file per concern) | resources, data sources, modules, locals |
| `outputs.tf` | `output {}` blocks |
| `*.turf.hcl` | Turf overlays: `action` and top-level `action_trigger` blocks, which tofu and terraform ignore |

- **Record the why as a comment** above the block it explains — the request, constraint or policy behind it. Nothing else carries it across sessions.
- **Reference, don't copy.** Wire values with expressions (`aws_vpc.main.id`, `module.net.subnet_ids`): a computed value is unknown until applied, and a pasted literal goes stale.
- **A provider with no settings needs no block**; every aliased instance needs its own. Provider blocks belong in the root module only ([`references/providers.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/providers/)).
- **Keep the backend's non-secret settings in the file**, so a reopen needs nothing but credentials.
- **Root outputs persist; module outputs do not.** To keep a value — an endpoint, a generated name — make it a root `output`; `output` reads it any time.

### Secrets never go in a file

- **Provider credentials** → the engine's environment ([`skill_deployment → references/credentials.md`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/credentials/)), or a `variable` (`sensitive = true`, plus `ephemeral = true` when it only feeds provider blocks and write-only arguments) passed as `var` on each plan command.
- **Backend credentials** → out of the `backend` block, into `open`'s `backend_config`.
- **A secret a resource needs** → only a **write-only argument** (`write_only` in `provider_describe`), fed by an ephemeral variable or an `ephemeral` resource. Anything else keeps the secret in state forever; if there is no write-only argument, say so.

Precedence, validation and module inputs: [`references/variables.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/variables/).

## Expression syntax

| Form | Resolved |
|---|---|
| `var.region` | at plan |
| `aws_vpc.main.id` | at plan where known; otherwise unknown until applied, and what needs it at plan defers a round |
| `data.aws_ami.latest.id` | when the plan reads the data source (every plan reads every declared one) |
| `ephemeral.vault_kv_secret_v2.db.data.password` | when the plan opens it; never stored — only a write-only argument or a provider block may take it |
| `module.net.subnet_ids` | as the module's output resolves |

Unknowns print as `__cty_unknown__`, and sensitive values as `__cty_sensitive__`. A reference to something the configuration does not declare fails the plan, naming it; an output a module does not declare fails once the call is planned (*"Unsupported attribute"*), and reads unknown while the call is deferred.

## What Turf honours

Terraform semantics: resources, data sources, `ephemeral` resources, locals, variables with `validation {}`, outputs (a child module's may be `ephemeral = true`; a root output may not), `count`/`for_each`, dynamic blocks, registry/git/local modules, `depends_on`, `lifecycle` (`create_before_destroy`, `ignore_changes`, `replace_triggered_by`, `prevent_destroy`, and `precondition`/`postcondition` on resources and data sources), `moved`, `removed`, `import`, and `action` blocks with their triggers.

- **`depends_on` on a data source**: use it when the query's values are already known but the object they name does not exist yet. Turf does not infer that ordering, any more than Terraform does.
- **`replace_triggered_by`** says that replacing a host takes its contents with it ([`references/lifecycle.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/lifecycle/)). Nothing can infer that.
- **A local module source may climb out of the directory** (`source = "../modules/x"`), as in Terraform: sibling configurations can share a `modules/` beside them. It is read in place, from the directory the configuration's symlinks lead to, so it has to be wherever the engine reads the configuration too.
- **Refused constructs** — `check` blocks, conditions on ephemeral resources and output preconditions, provisioners, module `enabled`, provider blocks in child modules and more — fail the plan by name. Don't write them; if the user needs one, tell them. The list, each with its remedy: [`skill_deployment → references/divergences.md`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/divergences/).

## Changing what exists

| The user wants | Edit |
|---|---|
| Change a resource | edit its block → `up` |
| Remove it (and destroy it) | delete the block → `up` plans the delete |
| Stop managing it, leave it running | delete the block; add `removed { from = …  lifecycle { destroy = false } }` |
| Rename or move it | change the address; add `moved { from = …  to = … }` — a no-op, not destroy + create |
| Adopt something that exists | an `import { to = …  id = … }` block (reviewable in the plan), or the `import` tool |
| Replace it though nothing changed | `plan({ replace: ["<address>"] })` on the round at its gate — no edit |
| Tear everything down but keep the files | `destroy` — deployment; no edit |

"Remove" and "destroy" are different requests: ask which one the user means. **A delete of anything that holds data** — a database, a bucket, a volume — is the user's call before it is planned: offer a backup, or the `removed` block. Details: [`references/lifecycle.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/lifecycle/); adopting: [`skill_deployment → references/imports.md`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/imports/).

## Actions and interaction points

- **A checkpoint or an agent step in a rollout** — "ask me before the database is replaced", "verify the bucket is private after it is created", "tell the team when it is live" — is a `turf_action` bound by a top-level `action_trigger` in a `*.turf.hcl` overlay in the configuration directory. Its `target` reaches a module's resource by path (`module.db.aws_db_instance.main`). Tell the user which file you wrote: it is theirs.
- **For one rollout only**, pass the overlay in memory as `overlays` on the plan command instead of writing it.
- **An operation right now** — restart a service, run a smoke test — is `invoke`: no file at all.

Schema, events, `on_failure`, `condition`, keyed entries and the bare-token gotcha: [`references/actions.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/actions/).

## Editing files you did not write

When the user asks you to change a configuration they wrote: read the files first, make the smallest edit that does the job, keep their layout, naming and comments, and tell them exactly what you changed — add, change or remove, in which files. Prefer a new file for a new concern over restructuring theirs.

## The directory is the desired-state store

- **Durability.** Pass a real `path` to `init` and the work outlives the session. Omit `path` only for throwaway work: Turf allocates a scratch directory.
- **Reopen.** `init` on the same path rediscovers the backend, providers, variables and outputs; `open` binds the workspace and reports a convergence still holding it; `up` plans whatever no longer matches the state.
- **Not applying keeps file edits.** Declining a plan never reverts the files; use git when the user wants the edits gone too.
- **Agent memory** holds pointers — the directory's path, the backend and workspace, the user's intent, the *names* of the credentials — never the configuration, secrets, computed values or plan digests: [`references/memory-conventions.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/memory-conventions/).
